PRELIMINARY RESULTS OF A STUDY OF THE PALEOMAGNETISM OF THE SUDBURY IRRUPTIVE INTRODUCTION The Sudbury Irruptive has inspired a voluminous body of geological literature and yet its mode of orig in still remains enigmatic from many points of view. F i gure 1, a simplified geo l ogical map, shows that the irrup­ tive has a roughly oval shape composed of an inner member of micropegma­ tite and an outer layer of a bas i c rock commonly referred to as norite. The rocks of both members are known to dip concordantly toward the centre of the structure and they are presently believed to be about 1700 m. y. old (Fairbairn et al., 1968). Previous studies on the paleomagnetism of the irruptive by Hood (1961) and Sopher (1963) pointed out that the mean directions of magnetiza­ tion in the south and north sections of the oval diverge appreciably from one another. This observation suggested to both authors that the present shape of the irruptive is partly due to post - irruptive tectonic activity. Sopher had also noted that the paleomagnetic directions obtained from the norite are considerably more consistent than those obtained from the micropegmatite but he did not make a quantitative appraisal of this observation. Finally, he noted that within sect

tive indicate that the mean directions of magnetization in th e North and South Ranges diverge significantly by about 40 degrees, in conformity with the pre­ vious observations of Hood (1961) and Sopher (1963). A large proportion of th e paleomagnetic data previously reported by Sopher satisfy the norms imposed on the data reported in the present study and can legitimately be combined with them. None of the previous paleo­ magnetic interpretations can yet be disputed or corroborated in the light of the above analysis but their basis and the planning of future work to test them is undoubtedly established more firmly. In the East African volcanic material the only identified reversal that can be traced through a sequence of lava flows is that corresponding to the Gauss-Matuyama boundary. Mussett at the University of Liverpool. At each site a number of separately oriented samples were collected either as blocks or cores. In the laboratory several specimens were prepared from each sample for measurement under an astatic magnetometer with a maximum sensitivity of 9 x emu of moment per mm deflection. Trial specimens were subjected to the usual step-wise partial demagnetization procedure, and a best field selected for AF cleaning of the remaining specimens from each site. In general, soft secondary components were removed in peak fields of 100-200 Oe. The site mean directions after cleaning were calculated giving unit weight to samples. A number of sites were discarded because cleaning was ineffective judged by a random distribution of sample directions after cleaning. Others were discarded because they showed unusually large intensities due to suspected lightning strikes. The remaining cleaned mean site directions were classified into normal (N), reversed (R) and intermediate (I). In the East African volcanic material the only identified reversal that can be traced through a sequence of lava flows is that corresponding to the Gauss-Matuyama boundary. It is found in the caldera wall of Ngorongoro crater, Tanzania, and is fully described by GrommC et al. (1971). The remaining 240 sites are either normal or reversed, and for those younger than 5 My the question arises whether they can be used to provide information about the geomagnetic polarity time scale. In fact, long sequences of flows are almost entirely absent. The collection is largely composed of many short sequences, in many of which the stratigraphic order is not clear. Introduction The Late Cenozoic volcanics of Kenya and Tanzania form a vast alkali igneous province which extends northwards into Ethiopia and which spans a time from Miocene to Recent. This paper describes the results of a large scale reconnaissance survey of the volcanics involving 184 sites mainly south of the equator. Preliminary results from some of these sites were reported by Mussett, Reilly & Raja (1964), and a detailed account is given in an unpublished thesis by Reilly (1970). INTRODUCTION This paper describes paleomagnetic measurements and de- magnetization analyses of the Late Cambrian Point Peak Member of the Wilberns Formation of the Llano uplift area in Texas and compares the results with previous work. Paleozoic rocks thus are distributed in a roughly circular pattern peripheral to a central Precambrian igneous and metamorphic complex and represent deposition from Late Cambrian to Early Pennsylva- nian times. Structural deformation was primarily represented by gentle tilting of the strata radially outward from the uplift. Moreover, numerous faults exist, most of which are normal [Bell and Barnes, 1972]. The Wilberns Formation is subdivided into four members from base to top: the Welge Sandstone Member, the Morgan Creek Limestone Member, the Point Peak Member, and the San Saba Member. DEMAGNETIZATION DATA In the paleomagnetic laboratory of the State University of Utrecht core specimens (2.2 cm height, 2.5 cm diameter) were drilled from the hand- samples. The measurements were carried out on the very sensitive Czech- oslovakian JR-3 spinner. The specimens were subjected to standard altemat- ing fields for separation of the various magnetization components. No ther- mal cleaning was applied since these standard AF demagnetizations turned out to be most useful and adequate. Pilot specimens (at least one of each site) were progressively demagnetized in lo-15 steps up to the maximum obtainable peak value of 3100 Oe. According to the experiences with these pilot demagnetizations all specimens were partially demagnetized in 8-10 steps in the appropriate AF range. The characteristic and secondary magne- tization components could be separated and their directions determined with the useful help of orthogonal projection figures (Zijderveld, 1967,1975) which show sequential changes of the magnetization vector upon demagneti- zation. The Lower Cretaceous rocks consist of white and green, well stratified limestones with shaly intercala- tions, which are sometimes dark and bituminous. The Upper Cretaceous is exposed as white (Cenomanian) and pink to red (Turonian to Maastrichtian), well stratified, pelagic limestones, containing abundant planktonic forami- niferal faunas. The latter were sampled in a continuous section along the road from Quero to Schievenin (locality 1 in Fig. 3). Pilot specimens (at least one of each site) were progressively demagnetized in lo-15 steps up to the maximum obtainable peak value of 3100 Oe. DEMAGNETIZATION DATA In the paleomagnetic laboratory of the State University of Utrecht core specimens (2.2 cm height, 2.5 cm diameter) were drilled from the hand- samples. The measurements were carried out on the very sensitive Czech- oslovakian JR-3 spinner. The specimens were subjected to standard altemat- ing fields for separation of the various magnetization components. No ther- mal cleaning was applied since these standard AF demagnetizations turned out to be most useful and adequate. Pilot specimens (at least one of each site) were progressively demagnetized in lo-15 steps up to the maximum obtainable peak value of 3100 Oe. According to the experiences with these pilot demagnetizations all specimens were partially demagnetized in 8-10 steps in the appropriate AF range. The characteristic and secondary magne- tization components could be separated and their directions determined with the useful help of orthogonal projection figures (Zijderveld, 1967,1975) which show sequential changes of the magnetization vector upon demagneti- zation. We report here new paleomagnetic evidence bearing on this hypothesis, obtain- ed from sandstones of the Lower Cambrian Bradore Formation on Canada Bay, New- foundland. Isothermal remanence tests indicate that the entire natural remanence (NRM) of the samples resides in hematite. The mean NRM direction for 9 sites is D = 153”, Z = +52”, ag5 = 15’, confirming R.F. Black’s 1964 result from other Bradore exposures in northern Newfoundland, which he compared with rocks in New Brunswick. Although Black’s data appeared to support Wegener’s hypothesis, his samples had not been thermal- ly treated, whereas thermal demagnetization of our samples led to isolation at 665” C of a very stable component misaligned with the NRM direction. The 665°C component probably was acquired through a C(hemical)RM and/or D(epositional)RM process by the time the rocks became consolidated. After structural correction, this component corre- sponds to a reverse paleomagnetic pole at 29” N,167” E (dp = 3’, dm = 5’) 9 sites). Bradore sandstone from two sites located 50 km west of Canada Bay gave comparable (virtual) poles. This orogen is composed of rocks which contrast sharply with the cover rocks of the adjoining Canadian Shield in thickness, facies and structural style. Williams (1964,1969) classified the Newfoundland orogen into three main tectonic provinces, each characterized by a distinct geologic history: the Western Platform, the Central Mobile Belt and the Avalon Plat- form (Fig. la). Avalon Platforms of Newfoundland had been separated by a proto-Atlantic Ocean which closed in the Lower Paleozoic and brought eastern Newfound- land into its present position relative to North America. Williams et al. (1972, 1974) further subdivided the three tectonic provinces into eight zones, each characterized by a distinct Ordovician and/or pre-Ordovician history of de- position and folding. The westernmost of these zones, called zone A (Lomond Zone) exhibits a Grenvillian continental basement unconformably overlain by a Lower Paleozoic autochthonous succession, which in turn is covered by a stack of transported slices of Lower Paleozoic sedimentary and ophiolitic sequences. Williams and Stevens (1974) have summarized the evidence con- firming that zone A belongs to the ancient continental margin of eastern North America. In this pape

In Canada Bay the Bradore Formation consists of a locally developed basal breccia, followed by white to grey, green and light purple arkoses and sandstones, with occasional pebble con- glomerate. Towards the top of the section black hematite-stained sandstones and thin hematite pebble conglomerate predominate. The total thickness of the Bradore strata ranges from 50 to 70 m; for example, at Otter Cove the type section consists of 48 m of medium-grained, purple cross-bedded sand- stones overlain by 15 m of black hematitic sandstones. The following observations are due to Smyth (1973): the sandstones plot petrographically in the arkose, sub-arkose and orthoquartzite field, as de- 340 fined by Pettijohn (1957). The hematite grains are commonly well rounded to subangular and form up to 25% of the detritus, and the quartz grains com- monly have a black iron oxide coating. The observation (e.g. summary by Williams and Stevens, 1974) that vast carbonate banks lie along the entire western margin of the Appalachians, together with the fact that the Bradore sandstones in Newfoundland and Labrador are overlain by rocks conforming to Pettijohn’s (1957) ortho- quartzite-carbonate association, suggest that the rocks in the present study originated in a ti

the Appalachians, together with the fact that the Bradore sandstones in Newfoundland and Labrador are overlain by rocks conforming to Pettijohn’s (1957) ortho- quartzite-carbonate association, suggest that the rocks in the present study originated in a tidal environment bordering a shallow shelf sea. The paleomagnetic interpretation will require a knowledge of the degree of severity and age of deformation of the Bradore sediments. lllthough much of zone A witnessed both subsidence and uplift during the deformations as- sociated with the Late Precambrian-Cambrian erogenic cycle and the more widespread Ordovician-Devonian cycle (Williams et al., 1974), the autoch- thonous Bradore unit remained stable until subsidence began with the Late Cambrian. The subsequent uplift of the autochthon along with the Long Range Complex probably occurred over a long interval between Late Ordovician and Devonian time and the presence of the only major fracture in the study area, viz. the Wild Cove fault, suggesting that the final move- ments of this uplift took place as late as post-Acadian (Devonian) time (Smyth, 1973). Two specimens from each Canada Bay site were chosen for pilot thermal demagnetizations, and three representative examples are shown in Fig. 3b. All specimens in the pilot run gave thermally discrete curves with blocking temperatures in the range 600-665”C. The magnetization decreases only slightly up to about 6OO”C, but is lost at temperatures close to 700°C. From the steep fall in the curves, which essentially defines the Curie temperature, it seems clear that the NRM is predominantly due to hematite. However the small decrease in intensity up to 600°C could be due to a minor amount of unaltered magnetite. Upon demagnetization the directions of all eighteen pilot samples moved progressively towards the southeast, and at 665°C be- came closely grouped with shallow downward inclinations. Further heating to 800°C effectively demagnetized the samples (Fig. 3b). All remaining specimens from Canada Bay were then thermally demag- netized to 665”C, with the results summarized in Table I and Fig. 2. In the NRM the within-site directional scatter is variable and is of the same order w less than the between-site scatter (Tables I and II).

Mode of acquisition We concluded above that the main remanence carrier in the Canada Bay samples must be hematite. The directional changes observed upon thermal demagnetization suggest that this carrier may consist of two components both with blocking temperatures above 600°C. Hematite in a rock such as sandstone may be either primary at the time of deposition, or it could have formed during or after diagenesis. Four broad types of origin seem plausible: Process 1. An original depositional remanence (DRM) carried by grains hematized prior to deposition. Process 2. Deposition with magnetite settling in a DRM-like process and becoming partly or fully oxidized to hematite at some stage during dia- genesis or lithification (Van Houten, 1968). This process, in which the chem- ical remanence (CRM) thus acquired by the hematite is aligned with the original remanence of the magnetite, has been termed a pseudo-DRM (Har- graves and Banerjee, 1973). The present study was initiated for the foregoing reasons and forms part of a broad, paleomagnetic investigation aimed at obtaining evidence on the hypothesis of a proto-Atlantic Ocean (Wilson, 1966). Four specific objectives are: (1) to extend and refine Black’s Bradore study through more detailed sampling and with the use of thermal demagnetization in assessing magnetic stability; (2) to obtain a new Cambrian pole position for Newfoundland; (3) to apply the new result in constructing a path of apparent polar wandering for western Newfoundland; and (4) in reexamining the possible rotation of that block. Isothermal remanence tests indicate that the entire natural remanence (NRM) of the samples resides in hematite. The mean NRM direction for 9 sites is D = 153”, Z = +52”, ag5 = 15’, confirming R.F. Black’s 1964 result from other Bradore exposures in northern Newfoundland, which he compared with rocks in New Brunswick. Although Black’s data appeared to support Wegener’s hypothesis, his samples had not been thermal- ly treated, whereas thermal demagnetization of our samples led to isolation at 665” C of a very stable component misaligned with the NRM direction. The 665°C component probably was acquired through a C(hemical)RM and/or D(epositional)RM process by the time the rocks became consolidated. After structural correction, this component corre- sponds to a reverse paleomagnetic pole at 29” N,167” E (dp = 3’, dm = 5’) 9 sites). Bradore sandstone from two sites located 50 km west of Canada Bay gave comparable (virtual) poles. These results are useful for a potential test of a post-Lower Cambrian rotation of western Newfoundland. INTRODUCTION Newfoundland lies at the northern extremity

he westernmost of these zones, called zone A (Lomond Zone) exhibits a Grenvillian continental basement unconformably overlain by a Lower Paleozoic autochthonous succession, which in turn is covered by a stack of transported slices of Lower Paleozoic sedimentary and ophiolitic sequences. Williams and Stevens (1974) have summarized the evidence con- firming that zone A belongs to the ancient continental margin of eastern North America. In this paper we present the results of a paleomagnetic in- vestigation of the Lower Cambrian Bradore sandstones in the Canada Bay area (Fig. l), which comprise one of the autochthonous units of zone A. Paleomagnetic results from the Bradore Formation were previously report- ed by Black (1964), who collected ten samples from the Highlands of St. John and used the results in comparisons with other Paleozoic paleomagnetic data from Newfoundland and mainland eastern Canada as evidence on the 339 hypothesis of rotation of Newfoundland; this is discussed at greater length later. Apart from Black’s study, no Cambrian magnetic results on Newfound- land rocks have been previously published, and indeed the record of reliable Cambrian paleomagnetic data for all of North America is still poorly estab- lished (e.g. Vincenz et al., 1975). The peridotite consists of harzburgite (80% olivine Fog,,, 18% orthopyroxene (enstatite), and l-2% chromiferous spine1 picotite) occasionally extensively serpentinized; some of the samples are composed of 50% or more of serpen- tine as in the case of the oriented sample 3-88-73, which is a serpentinite. Primary direc- tions of magnetisation show marked improvement in precision after correction for penecontemporaneous folding, and show a late Llandovery reversal in the sense R ~ N. The group mean directions of magnetisation is D = 243.5 ° , I = 47.5 ° (precision parameter k = 29). Petrographic examination confirms observations from magnetic properties that relict titanomagnetite (oxidation classes 3 to 5) is the remanence carrier in most samples. Hematite, probably mostly late magmatic in origin, is widely developed in all samples, but only the principal remanence carrier where it has thoroughly replaced the titanomagnetite. Low- coercivity remanence is apparently caused by weathering effects but there is no clear visible cause for secondary high-coercivity remanence carried by some samples. The mean virtual geomagnetic pole position is close to Upper Silurian/Lower Devonian pole positions from other parts of Britain and defines a minimum apparent polar shift of 60 ° between late Ordovician and Upper Llandovery times. y data from small amounts of material. This applies particularly to the shift under examination here. Ordovician rocks from Britain yield poles near 0°E, 10°S while Upper Silurian and Lower Devonian rocks yield poles in the vicinity of 325°E, 0°S [1]. Both of these groups of poles are now well established but the timing and magnitude of movement between them is not well defined because of the virtual ab- sence of Silurian igneous rocks within Britain. Ex- ceptions to this rule are exposures of volcanic rocks in Somersetshire and Gloucestershire, an investiga- tion of which forms the subject of this note. 2. As part of the geologic investigations of titaniferous deposits of Canada, Rose (1969, 1972) reported some results of preliminary remanent magnetism measurements of titani- ferous deposits associated with Indian Head and Steel Mountain anorthosites. His conclusions in part were that, in the Steel Mountain area, the remanent magnetism of titaniferous deposits is randomly oriented and subordinate to induced magnetism, reflecting the instability of magne- tization of the deposits. In the Indian Head area, remanent magnetism is also not strongly retained in the titaniferous magnetite and gab- broic anorthosites. Recent geological work indicates an age of 1700 m.y., but this is not yet known with certainty. Results from 29 sampling sites stratigraphically covering the Tochatwi Formation are presented. Standard paleomagnetic techniques indicate that post- folding remagnetization is common, and this is confirmed by analysis of the magnetic vectors removed as partial thermal demagnetization proceeds. The N section lies about 14 km east of the other sections (Fig. 1). It spans the entire Tochatwi Formation, which at this locality is approximately 600 m thick. The A and G sections each contain one site in igneous rocks probably intruded during the Mackenzie igneous events at about 1200 m.y. (Fahrig and Jones 1969); site AA is located in a 1.5 m thick shallowly dipping intrusive sheet cutting Tochatwi rocks; site AB is a baked contact less than 0.5 m from this intrusion; sites AD, AC, AE, and AF lie roughly 25, 75, 125, and more than 200 m away from the contact. As these distances were measured horizontally across the outcrop and as the sheet dips at about 20" their perpendicular separation from the intrusion is difficult to determine, but is likely to be con- siderably less than the figures given. In fact, if the sheet was originally irregular in the area from which it is now eroded the separation is un- known. Indeed, in a recent review, Baag and Helsley (1974, p. 3308) concluded that "most paleomagnetic literature concerning red beds supports the view that the stable primary NRM of red beds was acquired at and/or soon after deposition". Furthermore, these authors point out that the presence of a gradual trend of intermediate directions between opposed polarity zones favours syndepositional acquisition of remanence. Despite these favour- able points, it is, of course, possible to devise later remagnetization schemes (e.g., movement of an isotherm or chemical front) that could give rise to the observed facts, and the problem cannot be completely resolved by reference to the Stark Formation data alone. The possibly primary nature of the remanence was discussed further in a companion paper (Evans and Bingham 1975), where results from strati- graphically adjacent formations were described. There it is shown that the remanence does in- deed pre-date the folding which, in turn, pre- dates deposition of the overlying Et-then Group. Since the stratigraphy in some of these basins is well known and since some of the formations consist primarily of red beds, these basins provide good access to portions of the Precambrian paleomagnetic record for North America. The present study is part of a program of paleomagnetic sampling of Lower Proterozoic rocks preserved in the East Arm Fold Belt of Great Slave Lake, N.W.T. This foldbelt lies within the Churchill Province and is bounded on the north by the Slave Province of the Cana- dian Shield. The nearby granites of the former province are Hudsonian in age (1450-2010 m.y.); those of the latter are of Kenoran age (2300- 2640 m.y.) (Hoffman 1969). The 12 000 strati- graphic metres of sedimentary and volcanic *Present address: Beckton Stock Farm, Route 2, Sheridan, Wyoming 82801, U.S.A. rocks comprising the Great Slave Supergroup have been mapped by Stockwell (1936) and more recently by Hoffman (1968, 1969), whose nomen- clature is followed here. Unconformably over- lying the Great Slave Supergroup are strata of the Et-then Group, whereas the final geological element consists of diabase dykes and sills correlated with the Mackenzie igneous events (- 1200 m.y.). The Great Slave Supergroup has been sub- divided by Hoffman (1968) into four groups: in order of decreasing age these are the Sosan, Kahochella, Pethei, and Christie Bay Groups. The Stark Formation is the lowest member of the Christie Bay Group, and it consists of at least 600 m of finely bedded red mudstones. Frequent discontinuous pale green layers and blotches up to a few centimetres thick give outcrops a striped appearance. Ripple marks, cross bedding, and hopper-shaped halite crystal casts are common. Because of the prevalence of polycyclic deformation and metamorphism in the Precam- brian, however, there are still relatively few rock units for which the ages of magnetization (as distinct from the depositional age or the metamorphic age of the rock) is known with confidence. Surrounding the intru- sion is a thermal contact aureole up to several kilometres wide, which is especially well de- veloped in pelitic and semi-pelitic rocks of the Petscapiskau Group along the southern and eastern margin. The intrusion has not been sub- 'Contribution of the Earth Physics Branch No. 602. jected to any significant regional deformation or metamorphism since consolidation. Recent isotopic age determinations have de- fined the time of emplacement and cooling of the Michikamau Intrusion fairly closely. A K-Ar hornblende age from marginal gabbro yielded - 1479 + 101 Ma (GSC 73-164, Wanless et al. 1974). A U-Pb zircon age of - 1460 Ma (with an error of a few Ma) has been determined by Krogh and Davis (1973) from a sample of adamellite, the youngest member of the intrusive suite. Biotite from anorthosite gave a K-Ar age of - 1400 + 50 Ma (GSC 63-164, Wanless et al. 1965). Together, these ages imply that the in- trusion was emplaced about - 1460 Ma, and final cooling to low temperatures could con- ceivably have been extended until about - 1400 Ma. Over 60% of the remanence is retained at 600°C, showing that hematite (presumably with a small proportion of ilmenite in solid solution) is the dominant carrier of the rem- anence. This was confirmed by a study of polished sections that show many large mag- netite grains up to 1000 pm in diameter, with and without ilmenite lamellae; large ilmenite grains of comparable size, with fine elongate lamellae of hematite; and numerous small aniso- tropic grains that are probably hematite. The magnetite grains are too large to retain a stable remanence so that the latter two types of grains very probably carry most of the remanence. A further example is illustrated in Fig. 4, although at this site, additional more complex magnetiza- tions are also present. One specimen underwent complete reversal during AF demagnetization. The westerly component, which comprises over 90% of the magnetization, has remanent co- ercivities of 750 0e or less and is therefore probably due to magnetite. Introduction and sampling In a previous paper [1] we presented some palaeo- magnetic results from the Triassic-Jurassic Isalo Group, the youngest group comprising the Malagasy Karroo Supergroup. In this paper we present results from the underlying Sakoa and Sakamena Groups; they reinforce our previous conclusions regarding the palaeoposition of Madagascar adjacent to Africa in the supercontinent of Gondwanaland. The geology of Madagascar has recently been re- viewed by Besairie [2] who has also provided a more detailed description of the sedimentary sequences of the island [3]. The Karroo Supergroup forms a con- tinuous north-south sedimentary belt on the western side, transgressively overlying the Precambrian crystal- line basement eastwards (see inset of Fig. 1). Sakoa Group of Madagascar. Secondary magnetizations could only be removed successfully through thermal demagnetization procedures and then only if the cleaning process was completed by 450°C. Heating in air caused extensive magnetochemical changes to occur above this temperature. Coercivity spectrum analysis and low-temperature characteristics of the heated and unheated green sediments indicate that considerable amounts of fine-grained single-domain magnetite are formed at 500°C or more from some non-magnetic mineral, probably the iron silicates. For this reason consistent palaeomagnetic data could only be obtained from about half the samples collected. Results from 4 sites (19 samples) of the Lower Sakamena Group give a palaeomagnetic pole at 64.9S, 113.9E (A 9s = 5.6 °) and 3 sites (16 samples) from the Glacial Series of the Sakoa Group give a pole at 47.9S, 84.1E (A9s = 8.1°). When compared with corresponding data from Africa these results confirm and strengthen our previous conclusions from the.Triassic-Jurassic Isalo Group regarding the palaeoposition of Madagascar. All three poles are only consistent with the Smith and HaUam reconstruction which places Madagascar off the eastern coast of Africa adjacent to Kenya and Tanzania. 1. Introduction and sampling In a previous paper [1] we presented some palaeo- magnetic results from the Triassic-Jurassic Isalo Group, the youngest group comprising the Malagasy Karroo Supergroup. In this paper we present results from the underlying Sakoa and Sakamena Groups; they reinforce our previous conclusions regarding the palaeoposition of Madagascar adjacent to Africa in the supercontinent of Gondwanaland. The geology of Madagascar has recently been re- viewed by Besairie [2] who has also provided a more detailed description of the sedimentary sequences of the island [3]. The Karroo Supergroup forms a con- tinuous north-south sedimentary belt on the western side, transgressively overlying the Precambrian crystal- line basement eastwards (see inset of Fig. 1). The Nagssugtoqidian metamorphism took place in early Proterozoic times. Distinct phases have now been distinguished within this metamorphism [1,2]. Then two sets of dolerite dykes were emplaced, a sparse east-west swarm followed by the extensive Kang~miut dykes. About 20 km to the north of Itivdleq (typically in Sagdlerssuaq) a later Nagssugtoqidian event, Nag 2, has been recognized which deformed and metamor- phosed the dykes into strongly sheared amphibolites. Both these phases took place whilst the rocks were still at high temperatures and ductile [2]. The his- tory of the Sagdlerssuaq area is complicated by ductile overthrusting but this was absent in Itivdleq fiord [3]. After the field work a specimen about 2½ cm long was cut from each sam- pie. Measurements of the intensity and direction of magnetization were all made on the PAR SM.2 spin- ner magnetometer. Magnetic cleaning was effected mainly by progressive altemating field (AF) demagne- tization, whilst specimens tumbled about three axes, with the Earth's field annulled to an accuracy of -+20 gammas. A limited amount of cleaning by ther- mal demagnetization has also been done. 2.2. Sagdlerssuaq The island of Sagdlerssuaq consists of strongly foliated acid and basic gneisses formed in amphibolite facies by Nag 2. The sampling was concentrated on five basic bands which may originally have been Kangamiut dykes; these are generally about 10 cm wide but some of them have widths of a few metres. The specimens from four of these bands yielded very well-grouped natural remanent magnetization direc- tions but the fifth was less well.grouped. New information on the age of the volcanics from the Colli Euganei and Monti Lessini (Northern Italy) collected by Channell et al. (1978) show that the divisions made by Soffel (1972, 1974, 1975a) of palaeomagnetic directions from the two areas into Eocene and Oligocene groups had to be modified. From the data of both sampling areas alone an anticlockwise rotation of the area between Eocene and Oligocene can no longer be clearly demonstrated. However, a combination of the predominantly Oligocene data from the Colli Euganei with the predominently Eocene data from the Monti Lessini as well as their comparison with corresponding p;ilaeomagnetic data f

as alone an anticlockwise rotation of the area between Eocene and Oligocene can no longer be clearly demonstrated. However, a combination of the predominantly Oligocene data from the Colli Euganei with the predominently Eocene data from the Monti Lessini as well as their comparison with corresponding p;ilaeomagnetic data from Stable Europe brings enough statistical evidence for an anticlockwise rotation of the area of at least 20-30° between Upper Eocene and Lower to Middle Oligocene. Key words: Palaeomagnetism - Age of Volcanism - Rotation of Italy. 1. Introduction Channell, De Zanche and Sedea (1978) have presented valuable new information about the ages of many volcanic units which have been studied with respect to their palaeomagnetic and rock magnetic properties by Soffel (1972, 1974) in the Colli Euganei and later (Soffel, 1975 a and b) in the Monti Lessini in Northern Italy. In the area of the Colli Euganei with two cycles of volcanic activities (one in Eocene, a second in Oligocene) Soffel (1972, 1974) interpreted an extremely non-Fisherian distribution of remanence directions (225.5° > D > 122.3°) in terms of two groups of remanence directions setting a dividing line at about D = 180°. All volcanic units (some of them with radiomet­ ric ages around 33 m.y.) with

> 122.3°) in terms of two groups of remanence directions setting a dividing line at about D = 180°. All volcanic units (some of them with radiomet­ ric ages around 33 m.y.) with a declination D > 180° were classified as Oligocene, all with D < 180° as Eocene. A declination difference of about 50° was found between the two groups. With this working hypothesis, additional sampling was made in the nearby Monti Lessini, where many volcanics of Eocene age crop out, some of them 0340-062X/78/0045/0035/$01.00 |00000044|| 36 H. Soffel radiometrically dated as around 47 m.y. old. Also in this region an extremely non-Fisherian distribution of remanence directions was found (239.9° > D > 131.9°). Like in the Colli Euganei, two groups of remanence direc­ tions were postulated setting again the dividing line at about D= 180°. All radiometrically dated volcanic units of Eocene age and others which could be classified as Eocene from the available geological maps had in general declina­ tions smaller than 180°. Some of the volcanites with D > 180° could clearly be identified as Oligocene. However, some units could not attributed to one of the two age groups because of lack of detailed geological information available at that time. Some of the volcanites with D > 180° could clearly be identified as Oligocene. However, some units could not attributed to one of the two age groups because of lack of detailed geological information available at that time. The ages of some volcanic units from both sampling areas are still uncertain, even after the study of Channell et al. (1978). In order to avoid further confusion, their palaeomagnetic data have been left out from the following discussion. Simply because of lack of a sufficient number of unambiguous Eocene re­ manence directions in the Colli Euganei area, I agree with Channell et al. (1978) and their statement, that "a 50° anticlockwise rotation of the area between Eocene and Oligocene can no more be substantiated". An objective was to test the contemporaneity of this body with the neighbouring Egersund anorthosite of presumed age about 900 m.y. Two of the nine sites sampled were rejected, as the magnetization was dominantly unstable. At the seven other sites, this unstable component was either absent or it could be equally well removed by AF or thermal de- magnetization: after AF treatment, all samples from these sites were left with a very stableremanence, directed steeply upwards. This magnetization was probably acquired at the time of either emplacement or recrystallization of the farsundite. A magnetic test for anisotropy indicated that the stable remanence is misaligned with the ancient Earth’s field direction by about 30, apparently due to layering of the rock fabric. After correction for this aniso- tropy, thernean direction from the seven sites isD = 341°,I = —82.2°, k = 142, ~ = 5.0°, corresponding to a paleo- magnetic north pole at 43.3°S, 166.0°W, dp = 930, dm = 970, which lies on Spall’s European polar wandering curve. The Svecofennian Loftahammar gabbro (Rb—Sr isochron age 1,694 - 106 year) and Jotnian dolerites (K—Ar iso- chron age 1,245 106 year) in Sweden were found to have palaeomagnetic pole positions in close agreement with poles from other Svecofennian rocks in Sweden and Jotnian dolerites in Finland, respectively. Palaeomagnetism of the Svecofennian Loftahammar gabbro and some Jotnian dolerites in the Swedish part of the Baltic Shield. Phys. Earth Planet. Inter., 12: 51—64. The Svecofennian Loftahammar gabbro (Rb—Sr isochron age 1,694 - 106 year) and Jotnian dolerites (K—Ar iso- chron age 1,245 106 year) in Sweden were found to have palaeomagnetic pole positions in close agreement with poles from other Svecofennian rocks in Sweden and Jotnian dolerites in Finland, respectively. These results support Neuvonen’s apparent polar wandering path during the period from 1,900 lO~ to 1,300 106 year. A reconstruction of the position of the Baltic Shield during the (1,900—1,200) 106-year interval, based on avail- able pole positions, indicates that the Baltic shield was close to Greenland and the North American Shield and reveals a contiguity of North Atlantic geologic-geochronological zones until 1,200 106 year ago. 1. Proterozoic supracrustal rocks of southwest Greenland and amphibolite dykes intruding the basement possess a thermal remanent magnetisation acquired during slow regional uplift and cooling between 1800 and 1600 m.y. fol- lowing the Ketilidian mobile episode. Most samples from amphibolite dykes (mean palaeomagnetic pole 214°E, 31°N) possess a stable remanence associated with development of hematite during regional thermal metamorphism. Metavolcanics from the eastern part (eight sites, palaeomagnetic pole 230°E, 60°N,A95 = 15°) and western part (twelve sites, 279°E, 59°N,A95 = 17°) of Arsbk Island have magnetisations postdating folding and are related to K—Ar ages dating regional cooling (1700—1600 m.y.); magnetic properties are highly variable and partially stable re- manence resides predominantly in pyrrhotite. These results agree in part with other palaeomagnetic results from the northern margin of the same craton, and currently available palaeomagnetic results assigned to the interval 1850—1600 m.y. are evaluated to define apparent

Palaeomagnetism of Ketilidian metamorphic rocks of SW Greenland, and 1850—1600 m.y. apparent polar movements. Phys. Earth Planet. Inter., 13: 143—156. Proterozoic supracrustal rocks of southwest Greenland and amphibolite dykes intruding the basement possess a thermal remanent magnetisation acquired during slow regional uplift and cooling between 1800 and 1600 m.y. fol- lowing the Ketilidian mobile episode. Most samples from amphibolite dykes (mean palaeomagnetic pole 214°E, 31°N) possess a stable remanence associated with development of hematite during regional thermal metamorphism. Metavolcanics from the eastern part (eight sites, palaeomagnetic pole 230°E, 60°N,A95 = 15°) and western part (twelve sites, 279°E, 59°N,A95 = 17°) of Arsbk Island have magnetisations postdating folding and are related to K—Ar ages dating regional cooling (1700—1600 m.y.); magnetic properties are highly variable and partially stable re- manence resides predominantly in pyrrhotite. These results agree in part with other palaeomagnetic results from the northern margin of the same craton, and currently available palaeomagnetic results assigned to the interval 1850—1600 m.y. are evaluated to define apparent

These results agree in part with other palaeomagnetic results from the northern margin of the same craton, and currently available palaeomagnetic results assigned to the interval 1850—1600 m.y. are evaluated to define apparent polar wander movements. Two large polar movements are recognised during this interval with the possibility of a third at ca. 1800 m.y. Proterozoic supracrustal rocks of southwest Greenland and amphibolite dykes intruding the basement possess a thermal remanent magnetisation acquired during slow regional uplift and cooling between 1800 and 1600 m.y. fol- lowing the Ketilidian mobile episode. The geology, which has been mapped at a scale of one inch to four miles by Baer (1967), is complex and difficult to interpret because the area is underlain mainly by various ages of granitic plutonic rocks of similar composition with very few time-markers (Table 1) . However, there are numerous dykes, a few plutons , and some flows of basic composition in the area and it w as thought that paleomagnetism could help in classifying and dating the various periods of intrusion. Funda­ mentally, the procedure consists in deriving the pole position from the stable primary remanence direction of the pluton, dyke swarm or lava sequence, and to compare it with pole positions derived from North American rock formations of known age (e. g. de Boer, 1967; Larochelle, 1967 and 1968a). The rock units sampled are underlined in Table 1 and listed here in chronologic order starting with the oldest: (1) greens tone complex, (2) gabb­ roic intrusives, (3) green andesitic dykes, (4) granodiorite intrusives , (5) blue porphyritic dykes, (6) basaltic flows, and (7) brown basaltic dykes. Page V 1 3 3 3 8 8 8 10 10 11 11 12 12 14 2 4 5 6 7 vi 9 - V - ABSTRACT The Coast Mountains are underlain mostly by a complex assemblage of granitic plutonic rocks with few time -markers. The paleomagnetism of 533 specimens from 70 sites representing several geological units of basic igneous origin in the Bella Coola-Laredo Sound map-areas was studied to assess their value as time-markers. The geology, which has been mapped at a scale of one inch to four miles by Baer (1967), is complex and difficult to interpret because the area is underlain mainly by various ages of granitic plutonic rocks of similar composition with very few time-markers (Table 1) . However, there are numerous dykes, a few plutons , and some flows of basic composition in the area and it w as thought that paleomagnetism could help in classifying and dating the various periods of intrusion. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: map-areas span the Coast Mountains in west-central British Columbia (Fig. 1). The geology, which has been mapped at a scale of one inch to four miles by Baer (1967), is complex and difficult to interpret because the area is underlain mainly by various ages of granitic plutonic rocks of similar composition with very few time-markers (Table 1) . However, there are numerous dykes, a few plutons , and some flows of basic composition in the area and it w as thought that paleomagnetism could help in classifying and dating the various periods of intrusion. Funda­ mentally, the procedure consists in deriving the pole position from the stable primary remanence direction of the pluton, dyke swarm or lava sequence, and to compare it with pole positions derived from North American rock formations of known age (e. g. de Boer, 1967; Larochelle, 1967 and 1968a). The paleomagnetism of 533 specimens from 70 sites representing several geological units of basic igneous origin in the Bella Coola-Laredo Sound map-areas was studied to assess their value as time-markers. One is located in the northern part of Finland, near the town of Oulu and is known as the Muhos siltstone formation. This indicates that the two con- tinents could twice been parts of a single plate, once during the Middle Precambrian (1 900— 1 300 My) and once from the Silurian to the Triassic (McElhinny, 1973). Further studies will throw more light on the problem but as a working hypothesis one could assume that (2 200 My) the two landmasses were widely separated prior to the Svecokarelian orogeny, as is indicated by the differences in climatical conditions and paleomagnetic orienta- tion, but that they were forced together during the Penokean-Svecokarelian (1 900 My) move- ments. Palaeomagnetic investigation Approximately five block samples per flow or dyke were oriented in the field. From eaeh of these a single core was drilled in the laboratory. After measurement of NRM (natural remanent magnetization using a FOSTEn [1966] slow speed fluxgate spinner), a single core per igneous unit was progressively demagnetized in an alternating magnetic field. The maximum field strength applied, 600 oe, was reached in four stages (Fig. 3). Examination of plots of intensity against declination and inclination show that in the majority of cases the secondary component of magnetization is small, and removed in fields of either 150 oe or 300 oe. The remaining samples were then all demagnetized at these two field strengths. The direction adopted as the best representation of the field at the time of intrusion or extrusion was that at which the site mean had the lowest a95 and highest K values (see InveNt et al., 1961). These site mean directions of magnetization are shown in Fig. 4 a, b and the data is listed in table 1 a, b. Palaeomagnetic investigation Approximately five block samples per flow or dyke were oriented in the field. From eaeh of these a single core was drilled in the laboratory. After measurement of NRM (natural remanent magnetization using a FOSTEn [1966] slow speed fluxgate spinner), a single core per igneous unit was progressively demagnetized in an alternating magnetic field. The maximum field strength applied, 600 oe, was reached in four stages (Fig. 3). Examination of plots of intensity against declination and inclination show that in the majority of cases the secondary component of magnetization is small, and removed in fields of either 150 oe or 300 oe. The remaining samples were then all demagnetized at these two field strengths. The direction adopted as the best representation of the field at the time of intrusion or extrusion was that at which the site mean had the lowest a95 and highest K values (see InveNt et al., 1961). These site mean directions of magnetization are shown in Fig. 4 a, b and the data is listed in table 1 a, b. The cleaned magnetic remanences of seventeen hand samples collected at different stratigraphic positions of the Corumbatai Formation exposures (Passa Doia Group) in the Artemis-Piracicaba area define three reversals of the geomagnetic field. On the basis of the geological data and the present knowledge about the Late Paleozoic Interval of Reversed Geomagnetic Polarity, those changes of polarity are interpreted as evidence of an Upper Tartarian age for the Oorumbatai redbeds from the Artemis-Piracicaba area. On the assumption ofa geocentric dipole the paleomagnetic pole for the Corumbatai redbeds is calculated at 86° South, 294° East, 0:9 5 = 14°. INTRODUCTION The present knowledge about the Late Paleozoic reversals of the geomagnetic field (Valencio and Mitchell, 1972), generally known as the Kiaman Magnetic Interval or Late Paleozoic Interval of Reversed Geomagnetic Polarity, allow us to assign an age according with the polarity of their primary magnetic remanences to those rocks formed within the interval Upper Carboniferous-Lower Triassic. Obviously, this is only valid for those rocks whose Upper Paleozoic-Lower Mesozoic ages are supported by clas­ sical geological (paleontology, paleobotany, stratigraphy, etc.) data and holders of mag­ netic remanences originated during their formation. Seven of these hand samples have reversed stable remanence (Fig. 2b). Directions of the natural remanent magnetization of samples with normal stable remanence are fairly well grouped, but those of samples with reversed stable remanence are highly scattered (Figs. 2a and 2b). It can be seen by the shapes of the demagnetization curves that a wide spectrum of blocking temperatures is represented.
